doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Audience emotion and playing differently with age
summary: JoAnn on audience reactions; Al adapts around arthritis and says he plays some things better now.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Do you think that people when they come to hear Al play make an emotional connection?
Oh yeah. It’s gotten, it’s grown exponentially. That over, since Al’s gotten older, and is getting older and older and I’m make no bones about calling him old.

I don’t feel bad about it because he is. But it just seems like as he’s getting older people are reacting to his playing in a more emotional way, that a lot of times you have people, like, in tears. You know, just teary eyed. And they can’t believe what they’re hearing. And I think that for us baby boomers and people that are around our age group, it gives us some kind of like hope for ourselves that maybe we’ll, well hopefully we can be in a place — it kind of shows people what you’re capable of in old age. I think we’re all looking for that as we age. So I think that’s part of it. He’s got a lot of young fans, and they just think, oh my gosh, you should see the girls in their twenties [screeches]. And I love it. And he does have a lot of fans of all ages.

Yesterday I was listening to an interview with George Clooney. And he was talking about Rosemary Clooney, who was his aunt I think, and how she in her later career made different musical choices because her voice had changed a lot. Do you find that you need to make different musical choices when you’re improvising now?

Oh yes. Due to my arthritis. And she can tell you because we practice a lot. I thank God that he gave me the ability to change. See I can play many different ways. And on the © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

blink of an eye I know, don’t go that way. But you’ve got to be fast. You’ve got to be efficient with your technique. If you have a lot of technique and you lost most of it you still have enough left to take the other route. And she knows it. Now this is not egotism but a lot of the things I play better today than I used to.
And my improvisation. Even I like what I do. Now that’s not egotism, that’s professionalism. When I say even I like it, that’s means it’s got to be good or I’ll admit it’s not good.
